spine: For a CHRO building or defending a hiring budget: the cost-per-hire figure most decks still quote is a stale edition of a SHRM number, and even the current one is a blended average that hides two axes the budget actually moves on, role band and hiring volume. This article dates every figure in circulation to its edition and statistic, then rebuilds the number from the invoiced hard costs (30-40%) and the uninvoiced soft costs (60-70%), so the reader leaves able to state a current, sourced benchmark, calculate their own segmented figure, and say exactly what it excludes.
coverage_note: None left out. Four of the five expected topics get their own section (formula in section 1, benchmarks in section 2, factors in section 4, the internal/external and hard/soft breakdown in section 6). The fifth, the definition of cost per hire, is folded into section 1's opening rather than given a section of its own, because a standalone definition section would repeat the formula section a reader would answer the same way.

sections.headline: How to Calculate Cost Per Hire, and What It Returns
sections.job: Settle the definition and the arithmetic in one pass so every later section can assume both. State the SHRM/ANSI formula, name the current ~$4,700 non-executive benchmark, then run the same formula on real inputs to show it returning $3,667, $5,000 and $8,000, which sets up the article's case that one blended average cannot answer a budget question.

box_labels: The SHRM/ANSI formula: (internal + external recruiting costs) / total hires
The formula behind the figure: external plus internal costs divided by total hires
The same formula run four ways: $3,667, $4,700, $5,000 and $8,000 per hire

sections.headline: Which SHRM Number Is Current, and Which Is Stale
sections.job: Resolve the figure confusion this article is named for. Date each number in circulation to its edition: $4,129 to SHRM's FY2015 report published in 2016, $4,700 to the current release, and separate the 2025 averages from the 2026 medians so a reader sees why two accurate SHRM figures differ by roughly 3x. Ends the habit of quoting a number without its edition.

sections.headline: Hard Costs vs Soft Costs: Which Half Gets Invoiced
sections.covers: Breakdown of what counts as a cost (internal vs. external, hard vs. soft)
sections.job: Separate the two ways of splitting the number and rule out treating them as one. Define internal versus external costs, which is the formula's own division, then hard versus soft, which is a visibility division, and land the 30-40% / 60-70% split that makes the invoiced figure less than half the real cost, up to 2-4x salary counted in full. Sets up the two sections that price each half.
